To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) hard collisions are insensitive to the structure of the spectator partons, (b) the energy loss of a parton traversing a nuclear medium is small, and (c) the leading twist approximation is valid in most kinematical situations.
(i) hard partons do not interact with the nucleus, (ii) the nucleus does not interact with hard partons, and (iii) spectator effects in hard processes are very important in some kinematic regions
the energy loss of high energy partons in nuclei is small and that the nuclear dependence of hard collisions is dominated by leading twist contributions, with higher twist effects being small.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding hard collisions in the context of perturbative QCD.
the question of how the nuclear environment influences hard collisions.
understanding hard collisions in nuclei, and with the development of a theory which can describe these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have learned a lot from nuclear effects, and that we have much more to learn.
the QCD theory has been remarkably successful in explaining the data, and that we have learned a lot about nuclear effects.
we have not yet understood all of the nuclear effects in high energy scattering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nucleus is a complicated object, but that it is not as complicated as we once thought.
we are still in the process of learning how to use the nucleus to study QCD.
we are still far from a full understanding of the physics involved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the kinematical regions where they can be studied, hard collisions in nuclei are dominated by the same QCD dynamics that governs hard collisions in free nucleons.
the nuclear effects in high energy collisions are not always what one expects.
, in the context of QCD, the nuclear target is not a black box, and that it can and does affect high-energy scattering processes.
